title: Buffered Emit and Prefetch Scheduling — Prototype Design
content:
Purpose
This note proposes a prototype scheduler for improving prefill/decode overlap that we’re calling Buffered Emit + Prefetch (BEP). BEP aims to reduce tail latency for mixed workloads by staging inflight prefill work in small prefetch buffers and emitting decode tokens from an independently prioritized, short-lived emit queue. The design trades a small, controlled memory footprint for reduced blocking between prefill-heavy and decode-heavy streams.

Motivation
Observed problem: long prefill batches (large contexts, long prompts) can monopolize GPU kernel availability and stall low-latency decode streams. Existing microbatching heuristics reduce average cost but still suffer 95th/99th percentile latency spikes when a large prefill enters the pipeline during steady-state decoding.

Design goals - 1) Keep per-request latency for short decode streams low (< 50ms extra) even when large prefill batches are active. - 2) Avoid unbounded memory growth from aggressive prefetching. - 3) Keep kernel utilization high for throughput workloads. - 4) Make behavior predictable and debuggable for users (observable metrics and simple knobs).

Constraints and assumptions - Low-priority prefill work can be delayed up to a policy-defined soft-window (default 80ms) without violating most SLOs. - KV cache is kept in device memory where possible; moving large prefill KV writes off-device is costly but acceptable within limits. - We have fine-grained visibility per stream: estimated prefill token count, remaining decode length, priority tier, and a cheap kernel-time estimator from the profiler.

Key concepts - Prefetch buffer: a small region of reserved device-side staging memory (configurable per-server) where prefill key/value shards are materialized before being committed to the global KV cache. Prefetch buffers permit us to schedule kernel work in two phases: prefetch (lightweight KV materialization) and commit (full KV insertion). - Emit queue: an in-memory, prioritized ring that holds streams ready to produce tokens. Emit queue servicing is designed to be low-latency and can preempt prefetch commit work if a high-priority decode arrives. - Soft-priority lanes: streams are assigned a lane based on urgency score = f(remaining_decode, latency_budget, customer_tier). Lanes are soft priorities; they affect scheduling but do not guarantee enqueue ordering past enforced SLO cutoffs.

High-level flow
1) Request arrives. If it’s a prefill-heavy request (expected prefill tokens > threshold), it will be split into: prefetch phase (KV shard materialized into prefetch buffer) and a later commit.
2) Decode-long requests are placed into emit queue when they have tokens ready to issue. The emit queue scheduler polls at high frequency and attempts to service the top N tokens based on lane weight and current kernel availability.
3) When a prefetch buffer has completed materialization, the prefetch entry has an expiration timestamp. The commit phase is scheduled opportunistically: when there are idle kernel slots and no high-latency emit work pending, commit runs. If the prefetch entry expires (soft-window exceeded) before commit, we evict the prefetch or promote it to a background commit tier depending on policy.

Microbatching and kernel selection - Microbatch sizing: BEP prefers microbatches that align with the emit queue heartbeat such that emit servicing can steal prefetch kernel slots without catastrophic batch reshuffle. Suggested default: microbatch <= 8 sequences or tokens-per-step <= 256 depending on model. - Kernel selection: profiler hints (histogram of kernel time per sequence-length bin) guide whether to run prefetch in compute-light or compute-heavy mode. For models with expensive KV write kernels we bias towards delaying commit into batching windows.

KV cache considerations - Fingerprinting: prefetch entries carry a lightweight fingerprint to detect duplicate KV shards across concurrent prefetches. If duplicates detected, merge into single prefetch entry to avoid double commits. - Shard granularity: prefer smaller KV shards (e.g., per-layer or per-512-token window) inside prefetch buffers to make commits interruptible. - Off-device spill: when prefetch buffer pressure is high, least-recently-used prefetch buffers spill to host pinned memory with a rehydrate cost estimate attached to the entry. Scheduler treats spilled entries as higher-latency and avoids committing them during high-priority emits.

Stream priority heuristics - Urgency score components: time-to-first-token (TTFT) budget remaining, decode length remaining, customer tier multiplier, and observed error budget. - Preemption policy: if a high-urgency stream is waiting, the scheduler may preempt one in-progress prefetch commit if the commit’s remaining kernel time < preemption_threshold (default 20ms). Preemption is cooperative; kernel must support preemption checkpointing. If not supported, preemption waits until natural kernel boundary.

Fallbacks and graceful degradation - Fallback to baseline: if prefetch buffers fill beyond threshold or kernel preemption not supported on hardware, BEP falls back to the current microbatching policy that prioritizes FIFO plus small-batch heuristics. - Degraded behavior flags: expose metrics and an admin flag to temporarily disable prefetch commit throttling and force eager commits for throughput-only workloads.

Observability and metrics - Emit queue depth, per-lane serviced tokens/sec, emit latency p50/p95/p99, prefetch buffer occupancy, prefetch commit delay histogram, number of preempted commits, KV duplicate merges, spill count. - Traces: attach a short trace for any request that experienced prefetch commit delay > 2x median. Trace includes scheduler decisions and kernel selection rationale.

Operational knobs (initial set) - prefetch_buffer_size (MB), prefetch_soft_window_ms, emit_heartbeat_ms, microbatch_max_size, preemption_threshold_ms, shard_size_tokens.

Compatibility notes - This design assumes kernels that can: 1) commit KV shards incrementally OR 2) be aborted safely at checkpoint boundaries. If neither is available on a given SKU, we limit BEP to host-side prefetch bookkeeping and rely on microbatch priorities.

Prototype plan and experiments - Phase 0: simulator. Implement a discrete-event simulator that models kernel time distributions (based on profiler buckets), fake KV shards, and varying traffic mixes (90/10 decode/prefill; 50/50; 10/90). Verify emitter latency improvement at p95/p99 and measure commit-induced throughput loss. - Phase 1: small-scale runtime change behind feature flag on infra-canary cluster. Implement prefetch buffer bookkeeping on device, emit queue polling loop, and commit preemption hooks. Run a 1-week A/B test comparing tail latency and throughput. - Phase 2: roll to region with mixed customers and enable telemetry dashboards, expose operational knobs to SREs.

Open questions - What is the right default prefetch_soft_window_ms across model families? (LLama variants vs mixin attention models will differ.) - How disruptive will preemption be on current CUDA kernels where preemption is simulated rather than native? - Do we want tenant-level quotas for prefetch buffer usage to avoid noisy neighbors?

Next steps - Build the simulator (JIRA-ENG-2741). - Design the small device-side prefetch buffer API with infra (ticket: INFRA-PE-812). - Prototype the emit queue loop and basic preemption in a forked runtime branch (PR: github.com/redwood/inference/pull/1428).

Notes to reviewers
Please focus feedback on: 1) the proposed tradeoffs between memory usage and latency improvements, 2) feasibility of preemption on current kernel implementations, and 3) shard granularity for most models we serve.

Rough sketch (ASCII)
[ incoming requests ] -> classify -> { emit queue (low-latency) | prefetch buffer (staged) }
emit queue -> small fast kernels -> token emit -> return
prefetch buffer -> materialize small KV shards -> opportunistic commit -> global KV cache

End of document
